newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S. envoy holds talks on Bosnian local poll.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy holds talks on Bosnian local poll.

text.p: U.S. troubleshooting envoy John Kornblum arrived in Sarajevo on Monday to hold talks with Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders in a bid to resolve an impasse over Bosnia's hotly-contested municipal elections.

After landing at about 1 p.m. (1100 GMT), Kornblum was expected to meet members of the newly-elected three-man presidency in the Bosnian capital amid a growing crisis surrounding local elections due next month.
But Kornblum will meet the three men separately, dashing hopes that his presence might kickstart the work of the governing body.

The Serb member of the collective presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, arrived in Sarajevo amid heavy security to hold discussions with Kornblum in the U.S. embassy in the city centre, Western officials said.
Bosnian Serb leaders have vowed to boycott the municipal polls which are tentatively scheduled to be held November 23 and 24 under international supervision.

Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic said last week that the international community had asked for too many concessions from the Serbs and that local elections would not be held in the Serb republic, which covers half the country.

Rival Serb, Croat and Moslem nationalist parties view the municipal elections, which follow national polls for a presidency and parliament on September 14, as a battle for control of disputed territory.
Serb authorities fear they could be voted out of power by Moslem refugees who registered to vote in their former home towns.
Bosnian officials said Kornblum was also due to meet the Moslem chair of the presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, as well as the Croat member, Kresimir Zubak.

The Serbs declared their boycott after the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which is overseeing the elections, adopted measures designed to prevent manipulation of voter registration.
The OSCE said it would recognise registration based on a pre-war census but would not accept refugees signing up to vote in areas where they "intend" to resettle.

Kornblum also planned to press Bosnia's factions to speed up work in the newly-elected collective presidency and parliament. The Serbs have boycotted the inaugural sessions of the two bodies three weeks ago, citing security fears.
Speaking to reporters in Pale before leaving for Sarajevo some 16 km (10 miles) away, Krajisnik said he would not block the work of the presidency but would also not allow Serbs to be outvoted.

"I would like to emphasise that we have to do our utmost to avoid war happening again but we must have in mind the bitter truth that war broke out solely because of outvoting and inequality of peoples," he said.
"There has been enough war and people want peace but we cannot allow equality of (the Bosnian Serb republic) and our people to be put in question," he said.
The presidency has only met once and Serb deputies boycotted the inaugural session of the parliament this month.

Apart from Bosnian factions, a number of Western officials have called for postponing the local polls, saying the OSCE mission needs more time to correct problems that appeared in the general election last month.
If all three factions agreed to extend the mandate of the OSCE mission, diplomats said it was possible major powers might decide to postpone the local elections until the spring.
